lead: A survey line has no meaning until its direction is fixed against a north. Surveyors choose a meridian as the reference north, then record every line as an angle from it. The same direction can be written as a whole circle bearing, a reduced bearing, or an azimuth; all three describe one arrow. This chapter shows how to switch between those forms, how to get the reverse direction, and how to move between magnetic and true north. These conversions run through compass work, traverses, and setting out on site.
prereq: You need Unit 1: angles, scales, maps and topographic sheets.

blocks.text: Direction needs a reference. A meridian is the line through the observer and a chosen north. Four meridians are used. The true meridian (geographic meridian) follows Earth's axis and passes through the geographic poles. The magnetic meridian is shown by a freely suspended compass needle and points to magnetic north. A grid meridian is a line parallel to the central meridian of a map projection; it is a drawing convention, not a physical north. An arbitrary meridian is any convenient line chosen for one small survey.

A bearing is the angle between a survey line and a stated meridian, and may be written whole circle or reduced. An azimuth is always measured clockwise from a north reference, usually true north, so it is the same as the whole circle bearing from that north. Always state the north used, because a bearing without a meridian is incomplete.

A whole circle bearing (WCB) is measured clockwise from north, from 0° to 360°. A reduced bearing (RB) or quadrantal bearing is measured from the nearer end of the meridian, north or south, toward east or west. Its value is between 0° and 90°, written with N or S first and E or W last.
RB = θ in NE; RB = 180° − θ in SE; RB = θ − 180° in SW; RB = 360° − θ in NW
blocks.where: θ is the whole circle bearing in degrees; NE means 0° < θ < 90°, SE means 90° < θ < 180°, SW means 180° < θ < 270°, NW means 270° < θ < 360°.

blocks.text: WCB = RB in NE; WCB = 180° − RB in SE; WCB = 180° + RB in SW; WCB = 360° − RB in NW
blocks.where: RB is the reduced bearing in degrees from 0° to 90°, with the quadrant letters chosen first.

blocks.text: The rule is mechanical. In the north-east quadrant the WCB is the RB. In the south-east quadrant subtract the WCB from 180°. In the south-west quadrant subtract 180° from the WCB. In the north-west quadrant subtract the WCB from 360°. Reverse the rules when the RB is given. Keep degrees and minutes; 1° = 60′. A result above 90° inside an RB means the quadrant rule is wrong.

sections.h3: Fore bearings, back bearings, angles and declination

blocks.text: The fore bearing (FB) is measured from the station to the next point. The back bearing (BB) is measured from that next point back to the station. The two differ by 180°: BB = FB + 180° if FB < 180°, and BB = FB − 180° if FB ≥ 180°. Add or subtract 180° so the result stays between 0° and 360°. At a station B, the angle between lines BA and BC uses bearing BA (the back bearing of AB) and bearing BC (the fore bearing of BC).

An interior angle is inside the closed figure; a deflection angle is measured from the prolongation of the previous line to the next line, left or right. Magnetic declination is the angle between the true meridian and the magnetic meridian. It is east when magnetic north lies east of true north; then true bearing = magnetic bearing + declination. It is west when magnetic north lies west of true north; then true bearing = magnetic bearing − declination. With 5°30′ east declination, magnetic north lies 5°30′ east of true north, so every magnetic bearing reads smaller than the true bearing by that amount; the magnetic needle points to the right of true north.

Declination changes slowly with time, so maps state its year. Isogonic lines join places of equal declination; the agonic line has zero declination. Local iron and current are separate errors; see 2.2.

examples.question: Convert WCB 145° and WCB 250° into reduced bearings and give the back bearing of each. A line has magnetic bearing 40°00′ and the declination at that place is 5°30′ east. Find its true bearing and the true bearing of the opposite direction.
steps: For WCB 145°: it lies between 90° and 180°, so the quadrant is SE. RB = 180° − 145° = 35°. The letters are S and E, so RB = S 35° E.
For WCB 250°: it lies between 180° and 270°, so the quadrant is SW. RB = 250° − 180° = 70°. The letters are S and W, so RB = S 70° W.
Declination is 5°30′ east, so add it. True bearing = 40°00′ + 5°30′ = 45°30′.
The opposite direction differs by 180°: 45°30′ + 180° = 225°30′ true.
examples.answer: The reduced bearings are S 35° E and S 70° W, their back bearings are 325° and 70°, and the true bearings are 45°30′ and 225°30′.

traps: The reference letter comes first: S 35° E is correct; E 35° S is not.
An RB number must lie between 0° and 90°. If a rule gives 120°, you used the wrong quadrant.
For back bearing, add 180° only when FB < 180°; otherwise subtract 180°. Do not produce 500°.
Declination east is added to magnetic bearing, west is subtracted. Reversing the sign rotates every line.
When adding minutes, carry 60′ as 1°. 40°50′ + 5°30′ = 46°20′, not 45°80′.

quiz.a: The magnetic meridian is the line through a station in the direction shown by a freely suspended compass needle, pointing to magnetic north.

quiz.q: State the relation between fore bearing and back bearing.
quiz.a: The two differ by 180°: BB = FB + 180° when FB < 180°, and BB = FB − 180° when FB ≥ 180°.

quiz.q: Why is a reduced bearing never greater than 90°?
quiz.a: A reduced bearing is measured from the nearer end of the meridian, north or south, toward east or west. That quadrant angle is always 90° or less.

quiz.q: Convert WCB 300° to reduced bearing and give its back bearing.
A line has magnetic bearing 120°15′ and the declination is 2°45′ west. Find the true bearing.
A line has FB = 80° and BB = 265°. Are the two consistent? What does the difference suggest?
quiz.a: They differ by 185°, not 180°. The 5° excess suggests an observation error or local attraction; check the compass reading before using the line.

quiz.q: Distinguish a bearing from an azimuth.
quiz.a: A bearing is an angle from a stated meridian and may be whole circle or reduced. An azimuth is measured clockwise from a north reference, often true north; some syllabi use azimuth for whole circle true bearing.

quiz.q: A map states declination 4°E in 2015 and a change of 3′ west per year. Find the declination in 2025.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern total stations and GNSS report bearings directly from grid north, and software stores azimuths as floating-point radians, not degrees and minutes. National mapping agencies publish declination grids that change with time because the magnetic pole drifts. In engineering, a wrong sign on declination can rotate a whole foundation layout.
